disease.summary: A very rare inherited childhood brain disease that causes vision loss, seizures and loss of skills. There is no approved treatment yet.
disease.description: [MOCK] Neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis caused by biallelic variants in CLN5, typically with variant late-infantile onset.
synonyms: Variant late infantile NCL, Finnish type

headline: No approved treatment yet — but CLN5 disease shares a lysosomal pathway with 3 other Batten diseases
plain_summary: CLN5 disease is one of the Batten diseases. In all of them the cell's recycling centre (the lysosome) fails and waste builds up in nerve cells. That shared problem connects your community to CLN6, CLN3 and CLN2 families, their groups, a shared registry and a CLN6 natural history study. One related disease (CLN2) has an approved therapy, but it is not known to work for CLN5.

treatment_status.note: No approved treatment for CLN5 disease. The closest approved therapy, cerliponase alfa, treats CLN2 disease by replacing a soluble enzyme (TPP1); whether a similar approach could work for CLN5 is only a hypothesis.

disease.label: CLN6 disease

related_communities.why: Both disrupt lysosomal breakdown in nerve cells and both start in early childhood with seizures and vision loss.
differences: CLN6 is a membrane protein in the endoplasmic reticulum; CLN5 is a soluble lysosomal protein

disease.label: CLN2 disease
disease.summary: A form of Batten disease that starts in toddlers with seizures and loss of skills. An enzyme replacement therapy is approved.

related_communities.why: Both are childhood Batten diseases with seizures, ataxia and loss of skills, and both involve a soluble lysosomal protein.
differences: CLN2 is caused by a missing enzyme with a known activity (TPP1); CLN5's exact function is unclear
CLN2 has an approved enzyme replacement therapy; CLN5 has none
related_communities.caution: CLN2 disease has an approved enzyme replacement therapy (cerliponase alfa) because TPP1 is a soluble lysosomal enzyme that can be supplied from outside the cell. That success does not automatically transfer to CLN5 disease: whether CLN5 can be replaced the same way is unproven.

disease.label: CLN3 disease
disease.summary: The most common form of Batten disease. It usually starts at school age with vision loss, followed by seizures and loss of skills.

related_communities.why: Both lead to lysosomal storage and vision loss, and the CLN3 community is the largest Batten community with an established registry.
differences: CLN3 usually starts later (school age) with isolated vision loss
CLN3 is a lysosomal membrane protein, not a soluble one
related_communities.caution: CLN3 is a lysosomal membrane protein, not a soluble enzyme. Similar symptoms do not mean similar treatments: enzyme-replacement-style approaches are not expected to work for CLN3.

gaps.question: Does CLN5 loss affect the same step of lysosomal degradation as CLN6?
gaps.why_it_matters: If yes, CLN6 study designs and outcome measures can likely be reused for CLN5.
gaps.what_would_resolve: A side-by-side proteomics comparison of CLN5- and CLN6-deficient neurons.

gaps.question: Can CLN5 protein be taken up from outside the cell (cross-correction) the way TPP1 can?
gaps.why_it_matters: It decides whether an enzyme-replacement strategy is even worth exploring for CLN5.
gaps.what_would_resolve: An uptake-and-rescue experiment in CLN5-deficient patient cells.
